newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - June 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - June 23.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories Monday:
* U.S. President Bill Clinton urged critics of the tobacco settlement to view it solely as a starting point.
* CNET, a source of on-line information, is expectedd to introduce a service to compete with America Online, CompuServe and the Microsoft Network.
* The tax package proposed by Congress would benefit America's wealthiest families while poorer families would lose money, according to a study by a liberal research group.

* General Motors Corp is teaming up with Sony Corp's to try a novel approach to advertising at a suburban Detroit movie theater. Rather than running an ad during movie promotions, the car makers is putting their vehicles on display.
* The Group of Seven industrialised nations summit ended with U.S. and European leaders split on the issue of emission of greenhouse gases.
* Jacor Communications has emerged as a rising star in the radio business, helped by deregulation and a Wall Street-financed buying binge.
* A number of companies in Silicon Valley are looking to create games and other computer products specially designed to make computers and technology more accessible to girls.
* Michael Jackson's latest album, "Blood on the Dance Floor: History in the Mix," is being met lukewarmly in the United States, but is doing better overseas.
* The American Society of Magazine Editors is urging editors to avoid allowing advertisers to influence the content of their publications.

* American librarians are facing a dilemma in the Internet age: Should they use computer programs that prevent children from accessing pornographic or other offensive material, which amount to censorship they generally try to avoid?
* American consumers are holding off on buying that new TV set, fearful of buying a conventional set that might soon be obsolete with the advent of digital high-definition TV.

* Two former top executives at AT&T Corp find out what life is like after the leaving the telecommunications giant: Alex Mandl left last year to join Teligent Inc, while Joseph Nacchio joined Qwest Communications International Inc.
